1.s: Daniel and three friends, young captives in Babylon, refuse the king’s food and thrive on vegetables and water. God gives them wisdom.
1.d: Daniel and his friends were exiled about 19 years before the main exile, and chose vegetables and water to stay faithful to God’s law [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. Daniel’s name means “God is my judge”; Belteshazzar may mean “may Bel protect his life” [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].

2.s: King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, struck by a stone that becomes a mountain. Daniel interprets it: God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.
2.d: From 2:4 to 7:28 the book is in Aramaic, the international language of the time [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]] [[tosn:Daniel 2:4]]. The four kingdoms are often read as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, or as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece; the main point is God’s kingdom that will never be destroyed (2:44) [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].

3.s: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to bow to a golden statue: “Our God… is able to deliver us… but if not… we will not serve your gods.” In the fiery furnace a fourth figure appears with them.
3.d: The three stayed faithful not because they were sure God would save them, but whether or not he did (3:17–18) [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. Hebrews 11:34 speaks of those who “quenched the power of fire” [[bible:Hebrews 11:34]].

4.s: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree cut down; he loses his mind and lives like an animal until he acknowledges that “the Most High rules”.
4.d: Told as Nebuchadnezzar’s own proclamation: pride is madness, healed only by recognising God [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. Boanthropy makes a person act like an ox, and the king’s records are empty from 582 to 575 BC, which may fit [[tosn:Daniel 4:33]].

5.s: At Belshazzar’s feast a hand writes on the wall: “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.” Daniel reads it: weighed and found wanting. That night Babylon falls.
5.d: Nabonidus placed his son Belshazzar on the throne around 553 BC [[tosn:Daniel 5:1]]. At Belshazzar’s feast in 539 BC God’s holy vessels were defiled, and judgement came that night [[tosn:Daniel 5:1–30]].

6.s: Daniel keeps praying three times a day despite a royal ban, is thrown to the lions, and God shuts their mouths.
6.d: Daniel prays toward Jerusalem, as Solomon had spoken of (1 Kings 8:48–49) [[bsn:Daniel 6:1–28]] [[tosn:Daniel 6:10–11]]. Hebrews 11:33 speaks of those who “stopped the mouths of lions” [[bible:Hebrews 11:33]].

7.s: Daniel sees four beasts from the sea, then the Ancient of Days on his throne, and “one like a son of man” coming with the clouds, who receives an everlasting kingdom.
7.d: Coming with the clouds suggests the son of man is divine; Jesus uses these words at his trial [[tosn:Daniel 7:13]] [[bible:Mark 14:62]]. New Testament writers saw the son of man fulfilled in Jesus [[bsn:Daniel 7:1–12:13]].

8.s: A vision of a ram and a goat: a great horn is broken, and a small horn grows arrogant and stops the temple sacrifices.
8.d: The little horn fits Antiochus IV “Epiphanes”, Seleucid ruler 175–163 BC [[tosn:Daniel 8:23–25]], who defiled the temple in December 167 BC; it was cleansed in December 164 BC [[tosn:Daniel 8:13–14]].

9.s: Reading Jeremiah’s seventy years, Daniel prays a great prayer of confession. Gabriel answers with “seventy weeks” until an anointed one is cut off.
9.d: Many read the seventy sevens as 490 years, but the Hebrew does not say “years” [[tosn:Daniel 9:24]]. Some interpreters see it ending with Antiochus IV, others with the death of Christ and the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 [[tosn:Daniel 9:24–27]] [[tosn:Daniel 9:25]].

10.s: After three weeks of fasting Daniel sees a glorious man by the Tigris, who tells of a struggle with the prince of Persia.
10.d: Spirit princes over Persia and Greece resisted God’s messenger, but the world is governed by the Ancient of Days, who hears prayer [[tosn:Daniel 10:13]]. Compare Ephesians 6:12 [[bible:Ephesians 6:12]].

11.s: A detailed prophecy of the wars between the kings of the north (Seleucids) and the south (Ptolemies), and a king who exalts himself above every god.
11.d: The visions match the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings in close detail, for example Antiochus II and Ptolemy II [[tosn:Daniel 11:6]]. Scholars debate whether the book was written in the sixth century BC or around 165 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].

12.s: Michael will arise; “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame.” The wise will shine like the stars. Daniel is told to seal up the book.
12.d: One of the clearest Old Testament statements of resurrection and judgement [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. Daniel died before the end, but knew he would rise [[tosn:Daniel 12:13]]. Jesus speaks of the same two resurrections in John 5:28–29 [[bible:John 5:28-29]].
